explanation: Fires strongly on the 'A' of the 'A:' answer marker that begins the answer section in StackExchange-style Q&A dumps (after a question and a blank line). It fires much more weakly on other line-initial tokens followed by a colon (e.g. 'public:' in C++) and on the ' per' token in French/Portuguese/English words; ordinary prose tokens get little.

No clear shared feature. It fires moderately to strongly on scattered tokens: CJK characters and full-width brackets, digits inside numbers and ranges, slashes in URLs and paths, code punctuation (' <', ':'), and odd function words. It looks like a mixed or position/format feature with no single meaning.

Fires on the first token of a person's given name (often a partial subword like ' Jord', ' Rh', ' Hil') in running text, especially right after a role or context word ('teammate', 'coached by', 'said', '(c)'). Surnames, place names and later-mentioned or famous names fire more weakly.

Fires on chemistry and formulation words for mixtures, solutions and colloids: 'v/v' and 'w/v' concentration notation (strongest), dispersion/dispersant, emulsion, suspension, colloidal, solutes, and 'by weight'/'basis'/'dry weight' composition phrases. It mostly fires on the word piece that names the mixture type or composition unit.

Mixed. It fires on code and structured-syntax tokens (Elixir function names and parentheses, colons in headers and ARNs, '://', opening quotes and parentheses in calls) and also on the space token before a number in a list or range of numbers/percentages in prose (', and[ ]10%'). These two groups don't share an obvious meaning.

No coherent theme. It fires on scattered tokens in code, configs and URLs ('var', ':' before a port number, 'port', '.auth', 'validators', hyphens in case numbers) and on random prose tokens (' vein', ' assist', ' say', ' life', 'ates'). It is perhaps loosely tied to technical identifiers and ports, but the examples are too varied to predict from.

Fires strongly on a semicolon that joins two clauses in prose (often before 'however', 'therefore', 'see', 'either') and on a semicolon in 'text/html; charset'. Weaker hits come from clause-linking words ('that', 'who') and sentence-final periods.

Fires on words that refer to an outcome or state after a process: 'trained' weights, 'return result', 'the results', 'new values', 'serialized strings', 'created user', 'postoperative'/'post-op', 'after treatment', 'upon her return'. It responds to the word naming what comes out of, or follows, a previous action.

Fires on layout tokens in formatted document headers: long runs of spaces, multiple newlines, and the periods, commas or underscores that end lines in court opinion captions and in boxed license or copyright comment headers. Ordinary prose punctuation fires weakly or not at all.

Two jobs. (1) Pig/swine words ('porcine', 'swine', 'pig(s)', also the subword 'pig' in hypopigmentation/pigments). (2) LaTeX/Markdown scientific-paper markup: '[' and ' ([' before citations like [@B9], '[]' in theorem definitions, and 'author:'/'title:' metadata. The two share only a scientific-text setting.

Fires on a word that heads a quantity, rank or measure phrase just before its argument, e.g. 'incidence rate', 'effect size', 'one of the first', 'percent of', 'the nearest', 'the number of', 'frequency of', 'ticket price', 'final step'. It mostly fires in statistical or comparative contexts where a number or ranking is being framed.

Fires on the word piece right after a word-initial 'h' or 'th' in rare names and words split into subwords (h|ollow, TH|OM, H|ann, th|imerosal, h|ex, h|sv, h|olly, Th|om, H|AY). It is a spelling-level feature for continuing an h/th-initial token, not a meaning feature.

Fires on the second (head) word of a compound noun or technical term, completing a fixed phrase: 'reference POINTS', 'DOE cycles', 'Intelligence Tasks', 'Tax Return', 'executionOrder', 'composite design', 'Media caption', 'television schedule'. Strength depends on the compound context, not on the token alone.

Fires strongly on the words 'system'/'System', 'data'/'Data' and 'time'/'Time' (and similar generic tech nouns like 'input', 'State', 'Current', 'Get') when they start a compound or identifier in technical text, e.g. 'System.Media', 'data table', 'time_series', 'system reboot'. Other nouns fire weakly.
